Control Settings for Network Model Estimation and Simulation

Source: R/net.controls.R
net-controls.Rd

netest(), netdx(), and control.net() pass control settings to the ergm and tergm packages, which estimate and simulate the network model, through their set.control.ergm, set.control.tergm, and set.control.ergm.ego arguments. This page lists the control function that each argument takes, the defaults that EpiModel sets, how to use netdx() to find the stage that needs adjusting, and the settings most often changed.

The worked examples are in the Improving Model Estimation and Simulation appendix of the Network Modeling for Epidemics course materials, which covers full STERGM estimation for short partnership durations, the estimation settings for large and slow ERGM fits, and the simulation settings for diagnostics and epidemic models.

Where Each Setting Applies

Each argument takes an object built by a specific control function. Passing an object from another one stops with an error that names the right function.

  • Estimation in netest():

    • set.control.ergm takes ergm::control.ergm(), for the ERGM fit with the edges dissolution approximation (edapprox = TRUE).

    • set.control.ergm.ego takes ergm.ego::control.ergm.ego(), for the same fit when nw is an egor object.

    • set.control.tergm takes tergm::control.tergm(), for the full STERGM fit (edapprox = FALSE).

  • Simulation in netdx() and control.net():

    • set.control.ergm takes ergm::control.simulate.formula(), for the cross-sectional network that the dynamic simulation starts from, and for the static diagnostics of netdx(dynamic = FALSE). It is used only for fits with edapprox = TRUE; a full STERGM fit starts from the network saved by netest().

    • set.control.tergm takes tergm::control.simulate.formula.tergm(), for each time step of the dynamic network simulation, both in the diagnostics and in the epidemic model.

In a model with several network layers, control.net() takes one control object per layer through multilayer().

Defaults Set by EpiModel

Three defaults differ from those of the control functions themselves:

  • set.control.tergm in netest() is control.tergm(MCMC.maxchanges = .Machine$integer.max).

  • set.control.tergm in netdx() and control.net() is control.simulate.formula.tergm(MCMC.maxchanges = .Machine$integer.max). This raises the number of network changes that tergm can record in one simulation above its default limit of 1e6, which a long netdx() run can exceed.

  • set.control.ergm in control.net() is control.simulate.formula(MCMC.burnin = 2e5), a longer burn-in for the starting network than the ergm default.

A control object passed to one of these arguments replaces the default as a whole, not only the settings it names, so restate these settings alongside any others (see the examples).

Which Stage to Adjust

An error or a stalled fit in netest() calls for the estimation settings below. When the fit succeeds but the dynamic diagnostics of netdx() miss the formation targets, the cause can lie in the simulation, in the edges dissolution approximation, or in the cross-sectional fit:

  1. The per-step burn-in of the simulation. By default, tergm sets the number of proposals in each time step adaptively. With short partnership durations it can end a time step before the network has replaced the partnerships that dissolved, so statistics such as the edge count settle below their targets. This applies to fits with and without the approximation. Setting MCMC.burnin.min and MCMC.burnin.max in set.control.tergm to the same value (such as 1e4) fixes the number of proposals per time step and is quick to try.

  2. The edges dissolution approximation. For fits with edapprox = TRUE, run static diagnostics with netdx(dynamic = FALSE). If they are on target but the dynamic diagnostics remain off with a fixed per-step burn-in, the approximation is the likely cause. It loses accuracy when many partnerships form and dissolve at each time step, that is, when durations are short or density is high. Fit the full STERGM with edapprox = FALSE, or redefine the time step as a shorter unit so that durations span more time steps, rescaling every other time-based parameter of the model to match.

  3. The cross-sectional fit. If the static diagnostics are also off, the ERGM fit has not reached the targets, or the static simulation has not moved far enough from its starting network. On a large network, raise MCMC.burnin and MCMC.interval in the set.control.ergm of netdx() before changing the estimation settings of netest().

Read the Pct Diff column of print.netdx() alongside the Z Score. The standard error behind the Z score shrinks with the effective sample size, so many static draws can make a difference of a fraction of a percent statistically significant, while the autocorrelation between time steps keeps the effective sample size of a dynamic simulation, and so its Z scores, smaller.

The simulation settings that bring the netdx() diagnostics on target belong in control.net() as well: the epidemic simulation steps the network forward with the same tergm simulation, so without them it runs on the network that the diagnostics flagged.

Settings Most Often Changed

The control functions have many arguments, of which a few account for most adjustments in practice. Their help pages document the rest.

For the ERGM fit, in ergm::control.ergm():

  • MCMLE.maxit: the maximum number of MCMLE iterations. Raise it for a fit that is still moving toward the targets when it stops.

  • MCMC.samplesize, MCMC.interval, and MCMC.burnin: the size, spacing, and burn-in of the MCMC sample drawn at each iteration. Larger networks generally need a longer interval and burn-in. By default ergm extends the sample until it reaches the effective size set by MCMLE.effectiveSize; setting MCMLE.effectiveSize = NULL holds it at MCMC.samplesize draws, which bounds the time per iteration.

  • SAN.nsteps.times and SAN.maxit: simulated annealing (SAN) builds the starting network that matches the target statistics. SAN.nsteps.times scales the total number of SAN proposals, and SAN.maxit divides them into that many runs. Raise SAN.nsteps.times when SAN does not reach the targets.

  • MCMC.prop: hints for the MCMC proposal (see ergm::ergmHint). When most ties fall within a few cells of a mixing matrix, a stratified proposal such as ~strat(attr = ~age.grp) + sparse stops the sampler from spending its proposals on cells that hold few or no ties. Listing any hint replaces the default ones, so list sparse as well.

  • MCMC.maxedges: the maximum number of edges in a sampled network, unlimited by default. A finite value makes a fit that wanders into dense, degenerate networks stop with an error rather than run for hours.

  • MCMLE.steplength with MCMLE.steplength.margin = NULL: a fixed step length below 1 (such as 0.5) keeps the first iterations of a hard fit from overshooting. With the default margin, MCMLE.steplength is only the maximum step length.

  • parallel: the number of cores across which the MCMC sample is drawn.

For the full STERGM fit, in tergm::control.tergm():

  • EGMME.MCMC.burnin.min and EGMME.MCMC.burnin.max: the number of proposals per time step during estimation, set adaptively by default. Setting both to the same value fixes it, which can stabilize a fit that otherwise fails. In the course examples, 1e4 works for a network of 1,000 nodes, and larger networks may need a value on the order of the network size. Fix the per-step burn-in of the simulation to the same value.

  • SAN.nsteps.times, SAN.maxit, and MCMC.prop act as in ergm::control.ergm().

For the dynamic simulation, in tergm::control.simulate.formula.tergm():

  • MCMC.burnin.min and MCMC.burnin.max: the number of proposals per time step. Setting both to the same value fixes it, as described above. tergm has no MCMC.interval; this pair takes its place.

  • MCMC.maxchanges: restate .Machine$integer.max when passing any other setting.

  • MCMC.prop: the default, ~discord + sparse, proposes a share of its toggles (set by MCMC.prop.args = list(discordance_fraction = ), 0.5 by default) on dyads that have already changed within the time step. For strongly structured mixing, add a strat() hint as in estimation and keep discord and sparse in the formula.

For the cross-sectional simulation, in ergm::control.simulate.formula():

  • MCMC.burnin and MCMC.interval: the burn-in before the starting network (or the first static draw) and the spacing between static draws.

References

Krivitsky PN, Hunter DR, Morris M, Klumb C. ergm 4: New Features for Analyzing Exponential-Family Random Graph Models. Journal of Statistical Software. 2023; 105(6): 1-44. doi:10.18637/jss.v105.i06 .

Krivitsky PN, Handcock MS. A Separable Model for Dynamic Networks. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B. 2014; 76(1): 29-46.

See also

netest(), netdx(), and control.net(), whose arguments these settings are passed through; print.netdx() and plot.netdx() for reading the diagnostics.

Examples

# \donttest{
nw <- network_initialize(n = 100)
formation <- ~edges + concurrent
target.stats <- c(50, 20)
coef.diss <- dissolution_coefs(dissolution = ~offset(edges), duration = 10)
est <- netest(nw, formation, target.stats, coef.diss)
#> Starting simulated annealing (SAN)
#> Iteration 1 of at most 4
#> Finished simulated annealing
#> Starting maximum pseudolikelihood estimation (MPLE):
#> Obtaining the responsible dyads.
#> Evaluating the predictor and response matrix.
#> Maximizing the pseudolikelihood.
#> Finished MPLE.
#> Starting Monte Carlo maximum likelihood estimation (MCMLE):
#> Iteration 1 of at most 60:
#> Warning: ‘glpk’ selected as the solver, but package ‘Rglpk’ is not available; falling back to ‘lpSolveAPI’. This should be fine unless the sample size and/or the number of parameters is very big.
#> 1 
#> Optimizing with step length 1.0000.
#> The log-likelihood improved by 1.5495.
#> Estimating equations are not within tolerance region.
#> Iteration 2 of at most 60:
#> 1 
#> Optimizing with step length 1.0000.
#> The log-likelihood improved by 0.0794.
#> Convergence test p-value: 0.0001. 
#> Converged with 99% confidence.
#> Finished MCMLE.
#> This model was fit using MCMC.  To examine model diagnostics and check
#> for degeneracy, use the mcmc.diagnostics() function.

# Fix the number of proposals per time step in the dynamic simulation,
# restating the MCMC.maxchanges default that EpiModel sets
sim.control <- control.simulate.formula.tergm(
  MCMC.burnin.min = 1e4,
  MCMC.burnin.max = 1e4,
  MCMC.maxchanges = .Machine$integer.max
)
dx <- netdx(est, nsims = 2, nsteps = 100, set.control.tergm = sim.control,
            verbose = FALSE)
dx
#> EpiModel Network Diagnostics
#> =======================
#> Diagnostic Method: Dynamic
#> Simulations: 2
#> Time Steps per Sim: 100
#> 
#> Formation Diagnostics
#> ----------------------- 
#>            Target Sim Mean Pct Diff Sim SE Z Score SD(Sim Means) SD(Statistic)
#> edges          50   49.875   -0.250  1.436  -0.087         1.209         5.883
#> concurrent     20   20.885    4.425  1.054   0.840         1.266         4.530
#> 
#> Duration Diagnostics
#> ----------------------- 
#>       Target Sim Mean Pct Diff Sim SE Z Score SD(Sim Means) SD(Statistic)
#> edges     10    9.599   -4.014  0.305  -1.316         0.248         1.152
#> 
#> Dissolution Diagnostics
#> ----------------------- 
#>       Target Sim Mean Pct Diff Sim SE Z Score SD(Sim Means) SD(Statistic)
#> edges    0.1      0.1    0.481  0.003   0.161         0.006         0.042

# Pass the same settings to the epidemic simulation
param <- param.net(inf.prob = 0.3, act.rate = 1)
init <- init.net(i.num = 10)
control <- control.net(type = "SI", nsims = 1, nsteps = 50,
                       set.control.tergm = sim.control, verbose = FALSE)
sim <- netsim(est, param, init, control)
# }

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Estimation settings for a larger or slower ERGM fit
est <- netest(nw, formation, target.stats, coef.diss,
              set.control.ergm = control.ergm(MCMLE.maxit = 500,
                                              MCMC.samplesize = 1e4,
                                              MCMC.interval = 5e3,
                                              SAN.nsteps.times = 16,
                                              parallel = 4))

# Full STERGM fit with a fixed number of proposals per time step
est <- netest(nw, formation, target.stats, coef.diss, edapprox = FALSE,
              set.control.tergm = control.tergm(
                EGMME.MCMC.burnin.min = 1e4,
                EGMME.MCMC.burnin.max = 1e4,
                MCMC.maxchanges = .Machine$integer.max
              ))
dx <- netdx(est, nsims = 5, nsteps = 500, set.control.tergm = sim.control)
} # }
